rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.4 and 3 - the study runs its own multivariate empirical (MVE) stochastic simulations of lint yields and prices, validated against a four-year Bushland, TX field experiment (Table 1, Table 2), and conducts its own enterprise-budget and SERF risk analysis of MESA, LESA, LEPA and SDI at 25-100% ET replacement (Tables 3, Figs. 3-9).
rows.notes: The passage claims that micro-irrigation adoption reduces groundwater extraction only when the power connection is metered. The study contains nothing on power metering, electricity connections, or any institutional condition on groundwater extraction; it is a Texas High Plains economic risk analysis. What it actually shows: SDI gave the highest simulated lint yield at each irrigation level and a similar net return at 75% and 100% ET replacement, from which the authors infer (Sections 3.4, 4) that SDI 'could potentially' save irrigation water without compromising yield or income, while under spray/LEPA systems full irrigation remained most profitable and the authors suggest government policies and financial incentives would be needed to motivate water saving. Water savings are not measured as reduced extraction; they follow from the treatment design (less water applied at 75% ET). The metering condition is not addressed, so the study does not provide own evidence on the claim as stated; the citation appears misattributed (likely the metering finding comes from Bahinipati & Viswanathan 2019).

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Study is a simulation-based economic analysis anchored on field data from Colaizzi et al. (2004, 2005, 2010); the SDI technology matches 'drip', but the specific claim about metered power connections is outside the study's scope.
